newsitem.title: UK: How the bees replaced the birds to save mistletoe.
newsitem.headline: How the bees replaced the birds to save mistletoe.

text.p: A tiny bee may help save New Zealand's unusual exploding mistletoe by replacing the now-rare birds that used to be the only creatures that could pollinate it, scientists reported on Wednesday.
The lightweight bees have learned how to wrestle open the flowers of the mistletoe, which cannot open by themselves.

The mistletoe had developed a close relationship with honeyeater birds, which use their strong beaks to twist and break open the tightly closed flowers and spread the plant's pollen, ensuring its progeny.
But honeyeaters are becoming scarce. Plant scientist Dave Kelly of the University of Canterbury in Christchurch, feared the mistletoe would become scarce too.
In studying the mistletoe,9 Kelly and colleagues noticed the bees taking on the much-bigger flower buds.

"Tiny native solitary bees can successfully prise open (the) buds, which is to our knowledge the first documented case of an invertebrate opening an expansive, bird-pollinated flower," they wrote in a letter to the science journal Nature. The bee is not as efficient as the birds were in spreading the mistletoe pollen, but "still doubles the number of seed ripened per flower", they wrote.
The bee could end up saving the mistletoe, they wrote.
